I translate SAS programs to R for clinical trials. A trial's datasets, tables, listings and figures all come out of SAS programs, and the industry is moving to R. Each program has to be rewritten and checked against the original, because a script that runs cleanly can still produce the wrong numbers. That checking is thirty to fifty percent of the programming effort, and this year the FDA started asking sponsors for this kind of cross-validation.
So I built sas2r-agent, with Meta's Muse Spark 1.3. It writes the R, runs it, finds the numbers that differ, and repairs its own translation. This is the leaderboard, over one hundred programs.

One loop, four roles. The context builder reads the SAS program, its inputs and outputs. Muse Spark 1.3, through the Meta Model API, writes one R script. A sandbox with no network runs it. The comparator checks the outputs against the SAS reference and sends the differences back. Up to three tries.
Two programs. The first matches SAS straight away. The second doesn't: the comparator lists the missing values, sends them back, and the second attempt matches.

This is what a match looks like. The SAS figure on the left, the figure from the generated R on the right: same curves, same numbers at risk. Below, a statistics table, identical to four decimals.
Every attempt leaves a provenance trail: hashes of the prompt, the answer, the script, every output and the SAS reference, chained in an append-only ledger. Verify recomputes the chain.

The benchmark is one hundred public SAS programs, run in real SAS. Muse Spark 1.3 reproduces ninety-four. On the thirty-nine that produce datasets it matches thirty-seven cell for cell, the same as Claude Opus, and it passes three programs Claude misses, at half the cost.

The metric that matters is cost per matched program, not cost per call. Muse Spark is about ten cents. Muse Spark Open, the open weights, scores eighty-five on the same harness, so a sponsor can run this inside its own firewall.
The agent learns from its own misses. Here's a listing the first prompt got wrong: only four of three hundred and twelve numbers turned up in the R output.

The analysis of those misses became prompt version two: eighty-six to ninety-five percent. The remaining misses became version three. Each version is its own row, so the improvement is measured, not claimed.
Any cell opens the generated R, the comparison and the provenance record. All fifteen hundred scripts are in the repo, one folder per attempt.

Two limits: figures are checked for being produced, not compared, and one sweep varies by about five programs. The benchmark is my earlier work; the agent was built in the window. sas2r-agent doesn't just generate R code. It tests whether R reproduces SAS, and uses the evidence to fix what doesn't.
